blurb: Mutual fund distribution: suitability, discipline and service across the life of an investment.

subs.title: Direct vs regular plans and how distributors earn

items: Every scheme has a direct plan (bought straight from the AMC) and a regular plan (bought through a distributor).
The regular plan's expense ratio is higher because it includes the distributor's trail commission, paid as long as the client stays invested. Upfront commissions are not allowed.
The client's Consolidated Account Statement shows the commission paid and the expense ratio, so transparency is built in.

blocks.text: Talk-track: "Your money sits with the fund's custodian, not with us. We're paid a small trail by the fund house for helping you choose, invest and stay on track, and you can see that amount in your statement."
Investor takeaway: A distributor is a registered intermediary. Your investments are always held in your name with the fund house.
No fund is suggested until the client's goals, horizon and risk profile are written down.

script.title: The MF Distributor
script.text: Welcome to Module 1 of the Fund Horizon training series: the Mutual Fund Distributor. In this session we'll see what a distributor really does, and why our value is not in selling a product once, but in suitability, discipline and service across the full life of an investment. We'll follow the L.E.A.R.N. framework: Learn the basics, Evaluate the client, Act right, Review and rebalance, and Navigate behaviour.

script.title: Five stages of the client relationship
script.text: Every client relationship moves through five stages. First, we Learn: we must understand the ecosystem and our own role. Second, we Evaluate the client: their goals, horizon and risk profile, before any fund is mentioned. Third, we Act right: the right category, a clean onboarding and full disclosure. Fourth, we Review and rebalance: this is our answer when a client says "my SIP is running, what next?" And fifth, we Navigate behaviour: keeping clients invested when markets fall. That last stage is highlighted because it is where a distributor adds the most value.

script.title: Time in the market does the heavy lifting
script.text: Before we get into the role, here's why it matters. Take a simple ₹10,000 monthly SIP, and assume a 12% annual return purely for illustration. After 10 years, ₹12 lakh invested grows to about ₹23 lakh. After 20 years, ₹24 lakh grows to about ₹1 crore. After 30 years, ₹36 lakh grows to about ₹3.5 crore: roughly ten times what was put in. Notice that the last ten years add about ₹2.5 crore on their own. That is why our real job is keeping clients invested for the long haul. Every client who stops early gives up the most valuable years. This is an illustration, not a promise of returns.

script.title: Where the client's money actually goes
script.text: The first thing a client wants to know is: where does my money go? Follow the amber arrows. The investor's money goes straight to the fund, managed by the AMC, never to us. The fund's securities are held by an independent custodian. The RTA, CAMS or KFintech, keeps every record, statement and nomination. SEBI regulates the whole system, and trustees protect unitholders' interests. AMFI registers distributors like us. Fund Horizon sits beside the investor: we guide, onboard and review, but we never hold client money. Every trainee should be able to draw this from memory.

script.title: Who we are, and how we earn
script.text: A mutual fund distributor is registered with AMFI and holds an ARN. Anyone who deals with clients needs NISM Series V-A certification and an EUIN, which is quoted on every transaction. We are distributors, not SEBI registered investment advisers, so we never charge an advisory fee and never call ourselves independent advisers. On earnings: every scheme has a direct plan and a regular plan. The regular plan includes our trail commission, paid only while the client stays invested. There is no upfront commission, and the client can see what we're paid in their statement. Be open about this. Transparency builds trust. Suggested talk-track: "Your money sits with the fund's custodian, not with us. We're paid a small trail by the fund house, and you can see it in your statement."

script.title: Two questions decide the risk profile
script.text: Stage two is Evaluate, and no fund is suggested until this is done. First check the foundation: emergency fund, term and health cover, and costly debt being cleared. Then two questions decide the risk profile. Risk capacity: how much loss can the client afford, given age, income, dependants and horizon? Risk tolerance: how much loss can they emotionally handle? Look at the matrix. Only when both are high do we build a growth portfolio. If either one is low, the lower one sets the limit. A wealthy client who panics in falls is still a moderate investor. Re-profile after big life events.

script.title: Five discovery questions
script.text: Here are five discovery questions every sales conversation should include. One: what is this money for, and when will you need it? Two: have you invested before, and what happened in the last market fall? Their answer tells you more about risk tolerance than any questionnaire. Three: if this investment fell 20% next year, what would you do? Four: who else in the family is involved in money decisions? Often the real decision-maker isn't in the room. Five: what do you already hold, including EPF, PPF, fixed deposits and property? Talk-track: "Before we talk about any fund, let's understand what this money is for and when you'll need it."

script.title: The longer the goal, the more equity it can carry
script.text: Stage three is Act right, and the first rule is: pick the category for the goal before picking any fund. The staircase shows how much equity a goal can carry. Money needed within a year belongs in liquid, overnight or money market funds. One to three years: short-duration debt, arbitrage or conservative hybrids. Three to five years: balanced advantage and hybrid funds, with some large-cap. Seven years and more can carry the most equity: flexi-cap, large and mid-cap, index funds, and mid or small-cap within limits. Then choose the method: SIP from regular income, lump sum for long horizons, STP to stage a large sum into equity, and SWP for regular withdrawals. These are starting points for discussion, not recommendations.

script.title: The onboarding checklist
script.text: Before the first rupee goes in, run this checklist. KYC verified and not on hold. FATCA declaration done. Holding mode chosen deliberately: single, joint, or either or survivor. A nominee registered, or the opt-out formally recorded. Bank mandate set up for SIPs. The riskometer of each scheme shown and matched to the client's profile. Exit load, lock-in and expense ratio explained. Commission and the direct-plan option disclosed. And the reason for the recommendation recorded in the client file. Then set expectations honestly: "This fund suits your seven-year goal. It can fall 20% in a bad year. Are you comfortable staying invested if that happens?"

script.title: "My SIP is running. What next?"
script.text: Stage four, Review and rebalance, is our answer to the most common question: "My SIP is running, what next?" Every client gets a structured review at least once a year, in eight steps. One, a life update. Two, goal progress in rupees and percentage. Three, performance: XIRR against each fund's benchmark and category. Four, allocation: bring it back to target if markets have pushed it off. Five, overlap: if several funds hold the same stocks, consolidate. Six, step up SIPs with income. Seven, housekeeping: KYC, nominees and mandates. And eight, send a written summary of next actions. Talk-track: "Your SIP is on track. This year let's step it up by 10% and bring equity back to your 60% target."

script.title: A yearly step-up nearly doubles the outcome
script.text: Here's the single most useful review action: the step-up. Two clients both start a ₹10,000 monthly SIP and earn the same assumed 12% a year. One keeps it flat for 20 years and ends with about ₹1 crore. The other raises the SIP by 10% every year, in line with salary growth, and ends with about ₹1.99 crore. Yes, they invest more, ₹68.7 lakh against ₹24 lakh, but it is spread over rising income and they barely feel it. This is what "my SIP is running, what next?" should lead to in every annual review. Remember, the 12% is an assumption for illustration, not a promise.

script.title: Read returns right, switch only for a reason
script.text: Clients often misread their own returns. For SIPs, always use XIRR, because it accounts for each instalment's date. CAGR is for a single lump sum. Absolute return is only meaningful over very short periods. And to judge a fund manager, compare against the benchmark and the category, over three to five years, never on one year. When should we recommend leaving a fund? When it has lagged its benchmark and peers for three years or more, when the manager or style changes, when the mandate changes, or when the client's goal changes. Not because of one bad year. And always check exit load and tax before any switch.

script.title: March 2020: the test every investor faced
script.text: Every distributor remembers March 2020. The Nifty 50 fell close to 40% in about a month, closing at 7,610 on 23rd March. Phones rang non-stop, and many clients wanted to stop their SIPs or redeem everything. Yet less than a year later, by February 2021, the index had nearly doubled from that low. Clients who stopped or redeemed at the bottom locked in their losses and missed the rebound. Clients whose distributors called them early and kept them invested came out ahead. We can't promise any future fall will recover the same way, but this is exactly the moment where our value shows.

script.title: The investor emotion cycle
script.text: This is the investor emotion cycle, and every client goes around it. As markets rise, optimism turns to excitement, and at the very top, euphoria. That is when most investors pile in, exactly when risk is highest. Then the market turns: anxiety, fear, panic, and at the bottom, despondency. That is when most investors sell, often just before the recovery begins with hope and optimism again. Our job is to move clients against their own emotions: calm at the peak, steady at the bottom. When a client tells you how they feel, you can usually place them on this curve.

script.title: A falling NAV buys more units
script.text: Here's how to explain the SIP advantage in a fall. Take a ₹10,000 monthly SIP over twelve hypothetical months. The NAV falls from 100 to 70, then recovers to 108. Look at the bars: as the NAV falls, the same ₹10,000 buys more units, peaking at 143 units when the NAV is 70. Because of this, the average cost per unit is ₹85.6, lower than the average NAV of ₹87.3. And the result: ₹1.2 lakh invested is worth about ₹1.51 lakh, even though the NAV ended only 8% above where it started. The months that felt worst did the most work. That's why stopping a SIP in a fall is the costliest mistake.

script.title: The market-fall playbook
script.text: Stage five, Navigate behaviour, is where a distributor earns trust for life. When markets fall sharply, follow six steps. One, call first, before clients call you in panic, starting with recent and first-time investors. Two, reconnect them to their goal and horizon, not today's loss. Three, explain that their SIP is now buying more units at lower prices. Four, use history to show falls are normal, but never promise when or whether markets will recover. Five, act only if the plan says so: rebalance by rule, never make emotional switches. Six, record the conversation and follow up in writing.

script.title: When the client says…
script.text: Here are three things clients say, the bias behind each, and how to respond. "Let me stop my SIP until markets settle" is loss aversion. Respond: your SIP is buying more units at lower prices now, and stopping skips the part that helps most later. "My friend's fund gave 40%, let's switch" is recency and herd behaviour. Respond: let's compare both over five years and see how each did in bad years. "I'll sell when it's back to my cost" is anchoring. Respond: your buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next; is it still the right fund for your goal? And remember the ethics: never churn for commission, never push NFOs without a clear fit, never assure returns.

script.title: What clients miss, and complain about later
script.text: These are the niche topics that rarely come up at onboarding but cause the most service problems later. Transmission after death: a registered nominee makes the claim far faster than going through legal heirs. Minor folios need KYC updated when the child turns 18. A switch is legally a sale, so it can trigger tax and exit load. Each SIP instalment has its own exit load period and its own ELSS lock-in. Many fund houses let you pause a SIP rather than cancel it. With SWP, only the gain portion of each withdrawal is taxed. A ten-rupee NFO is not cheap, just untested. And the Consolidated Account Statement shows every folio across fund houses in one place. Cover these in your reviews.

script.title: A distributor's value shows up most when markets fall.
script.text: If you remember one thing from this module, remember this: a distributor's value shows up most when markets fall. Keeping a client invested through one bad year can matter more to their long-term outcome than choosing the so-called best fund. That is the job.

script.title: Dos and don'ts
script.text: Finally, compliance. Do: quote your ARN and EUIN on every transaction, describe yourself as a Mutual Fund Distributor, match the riskometer to the client, disclose commission and the direct-plan option, use the standard risk disclaimer with any past performance, record the reason for every recommendation, and share the complaint escalation path. Don't: deal with clients before you have NISM V-A and an EUIN, call yourself an adviser or charge a fee, sell above the client's risk level, hide costs, promise returns or recovery timelines, churn for commission, or ever handle client money.

script.title: Practise, then prove it
script.text: That brings us to the end of Module 1. Next, practise in pairs with the six role-play scenarios from the training manual, then take the ten-question quiz. The pass mark is eight out of ten. Our next module covers PMS Distributors. Thank you.

flash.q: Why is keeping a client invested the distributor's real job?
a: ₹10,000/month SIP at an assumed 12% a year:
10 yrs: ₹12 L invested → about ₹23 L
20 yrs: ₹24 L → about ₹1 Cr
The last 10 years alone add about ₹2.5 Cr, so stopping early costs the most. (Illustration only, not a promise.)

flash.q: What does L.E.A.R.N. stand for?
a: L: Learn the basics
E: Evaluate the client
A: Act right
R: Review & rebalance
N: Navigate behaviour

flash.q: Who regulates mutual funds and MF intermediaries in India?
a: SEBI. It sets the rules on categories, costs, disclosures and investor protection.

flash.q: What do the Sponsor and Trustees do?
a: The sponsor sets up the fund; the trustees protect unitholders' interests. They are an independent layer watching the fund house.

flash.q: What is the AMC's role?
a: The AMC (fund house) manages the money as per each scheme's mandate. The fund manager decides what to buy within the scheme's rules.

flash.q: Who holds a mutual fund scheme's securities?
a: The custodian. Investor money is not held by the AMC or by the distributor.

flash.q: What is an RTA? Name the two main RTAs.
a: Registrar & Transfer Agent: CAMS and KFintech. Maintains investor records, processes transactions, issues statements, and handles folios, nominations and service requests.

flash.q: What does AMFI do?
a: Industry body that registers distributors (ARN), runs investor awareness and sets the distributor code of conduct.

flash.q: What is an ARN?
a: AMFI Registration Number: the distributor's registration with AMFI, renewed periodically.

flash.q: What is an EUIN, and who needs one?
a: Employee Unique Identification Number. Every person who deals with clients needs NISM Series V-A certification and an EUIN, quoted on every transaction they handle.

flash.q: Distributor vs SEBI RIA: what can't a distributor do?
a: Cannot charge an advisory fee or call themselves an "independent adviser". Describe yourself as a "Mutual Fund Distributor"; guidance must be incidental to selling products.

flash.q: Direct plan vs regular plan?
a: Direct: bought straight from the AMC. Regular: bought through a distributor. It has a higher expense ratio because it includes the distributor's trail commission.

flash.q: How does a distributor earn, and how is it disclosed?
a: Trail commission from the AMC, paid only while the client stays invested. No upfront commission is allowed. The commission and expense ratio are shown in the client's CAS.

flash.q: What is the foundation check before investing?
a: Emergency fund in place (several months of expenses)
Adequate term life and health insurance
High-interest debt (credit cards, personal loans) being cleared
If missing, fix these first.

flash.q: Define risk capacity.
a: How much loss the client can AFFORD, judged by age, income stability, dependants, existing assets and horizon.

flash.q: Define risk tolerance.
a: How much loss the client can STOMACH, judged by past reactions to market falls, comfort questions and a questionnaire.

flash.q: Define risk need.
a: How much risk the goal actually REQUIRES: goal amount vs current savings and time left.

flash.q: Golden rule of risk profiling?
a: Match recommendations to the LOWER of capacity and tolerance. Re-profile after major life events. (A wealthy client who panics in falls is still a moderate investor.)

flash.q: What 4 things do you capture for every goal?
a: What the goal is
Amount in today's money
Target year
Priority: must-have or nice-to-have

flash.q: The 5 discovery questions?
a: What is this money for, and when will you need it?
Have you invested before? What happened in the last market fall?
If this fell 20% next year, what would you do?
Who else in the family is involved in money decisions?
What do you already hold (EPF, PPF, FDs, property)?

flash.q: Categories for a goal under 1 year / emergency money?
a: Liquid, overnight, money market funds, for stability and quick access.

flash.q: Categories for a 1–3 year goal?
a: Short-duration debt, arbitrage, conservative hybrid, to limit equity swings.

flash.q: Categories for a 3–5 year goal?
a: Balanced advantage, hybrid, some large-cap, for moderate growth with cushioning.

flash.q: Categories for a 7+ year goal?
a: Flexi-cap, large & mid-cap, index funds, mid/small-cap within limits. There is time to ride out equity cycles.

flash.q: What is ELSS, and what is its key feature?
a: Tax-saving equity fund with a lock-in that applies PER INSTALMENT. Suits long-term savers.

flash.q: SIP vs lump sum?
a: SIP: regular amounts from income; averages purchase cost over time. Lump sum: for long horizons when the money is available now.

flash.q: What is an STP and when do you use it?
a: Systematic Transfer Plan: park a large sum in a debt or liquid fund and transfer it into equity over 6–12 months, reducing timing regret.

flash.q: What is an SWP?
a: Systematic Withdrawal Plan: regular withdrawals later, e.g. in retirement.

flash.q: The onboarding checklist?
a: KYC verified (not on hold) · FATCA/CRS done
Holding mode chosen deliberately
Nomination registered, or opt-out recorded
Bank mandate for SIPs
Riskometer shown and matched to profile
Exit load, lock-in, expense ratio explained
Commission and direct-plan option disclosed
Recommendation and reason recorded

flash.q: How often should a client be reviewed, and what is the agenda?
a: At least once a year (30–45 min):
Life update · Goal progress · Performance
Allocation check · Overlap & clutter
Step-up · Housekeeping
Written next-actions summary

flash.q: Which return measure suits SIPs?
a: XIRR. It accounts for each instalment's date. Mistake: using simple or absolute return for SIPs.

flash.q: When is CAGR the right measure?
a: For a single lump-sum investment. Mistake: applying it to SIPs.

flash.q: When is absolute return meaningful?
a: Only over very short periods. Mistake: judging a 5-year holding by total % gain.

flash.q: How do you judge a fund manager?
a: Against the fund's benchmark and category average over 3 and 5 years, never on one good or bad year.

flash.q: 4 valid reasons to recommend switching a fund?
a: Consistent underperformance vs benchmark & peers over 3+ years
Change in fund manager or investment style
Change in the scheme's mandate or category
Change in the client's goal or horizon

flash.q: What must you check before ANY switch?
a: Exit load and tax.

flash.q: What does a 10% yearly SIP step-up do?
a: ₹10,000/month, assumed 12%, 20 years: flat SIP ≈ ₹1 Cr (₹24 L invested); 10% step-up ≈ ₹1.99 Cr (₹68.7 L invested). Illustration only.

flash.q: The 6-step market-fall playbook?
a: Call first, before clients call in panic
Reconnect to the goal, not the day's loss
Explain the SIP advantage (more units)
Use history, without promises
Act only if the plan says so
Record the conversation; follow up in writing

flash.q: In a fall, which clients do you call first?
a: Recent and first-time investors.

flash.q: "Let me stop my SIP until markets settle." Bias and response?
a: Loss aversion. "Your SIP is buying more units at lower prices now. Stopping skips the part that helps most later."

flash.q: "My friend's fund gave 40%. Let's switch." Bias and response?
a: Recency / herd. "Let's compare both over 5 years and see how each did in bad years."

flash.q: "I'll sell when it's back to my cost." Bias and response?
a: Anchoring. "Your buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Is it still the right fund for your goal?"

flash.q: Why does a falling NAV help a SIP investor?
a: The same instalment buys more units. In the training example the average cost (₹85.6) came in below the average NAV (₹87.3), and ₹1.2 L invested grew to ≈ ₹1.51 L.

flash.q: What happened in March 2020?
a: The Nifty 50 fell close to 40% in about a month (closed 7,610 on 23 Mar). By Feb 2021 it had nearly doubled from that low. Those who stopped or redeemed at the bottom locked in losses.

flash.q: The investor emotion cycle: when do most investors buy and sell?
a: Most buy at euphoria (the top, when risk is highest) and sell at despondency (the bottom, just before recovery). Our job is to move clients against their emotions.

flash.q: What must retention NEVER become?
a: Switching or churning for commission
Pushing NFOs or new categories without a clear fit
Assuring returns, capital protection or recovery timelines

flash.q: Transmission after death: what speeds it up?
a: A registered nominee. Without one, legal heirs must prove their claim. The claimant also needs KYC. Every folio needs a nominee.

flash.q: What happens to a minor's folio at 18?
a: It needs KYC and a status change to major, or transactions get blocked.

flash.q: Is a switch within the same fund house taxable?
a: It can be. A switch is a redemption plus a purchase, so it can trigger tax and exit load.

flash.q: Exit load / ELSS lock-in on a SIP: when are all units free?
a: Each instalment has its own holding period. The LAST instalment decides when all units are free.

flash.q: Client short on cash: cancel the SIP?
a: Ask about a SIP PAUSE. Many fund houses allow a temporary pause instead of cancelling and restarting.

flash.q: How is an SWP taxed?
a: Each withdrawal is part principal and part gain. Only the gain portion is taxed.

flash.q: Is a ₹10 NFO cheaper than a fund at ₹200 NAV?
a: No. New is not cheaper; it is untested. The scheme has no track record.

flash.q: What happens on a change in fundamental attributes?
a: When a scheme's mandate changes, investors get an exit window without exit load.

flash.q: What is a segregated portfolio?
a: In a credit event, a debt fund separates the bad paper. Investors hold units of both until recovery.

flash.q: NRI / FATCA points to check?
a: Some fund houses restrict US/Canada residents. NRE vs NRO account type matters. Confirm eligibility first.

flash.q: What is the CAS?
a: Consolidated Account Statement: one statement showing all folios across fund houses, including commission paid. Download it twice a year.

flash.q: Which small costs can change after investing?
a: Stamp duty applies on purchases. Expense ratios can change with notice and with fund size. Check them at each review.

flash.q: What must you quote on every transaction and communication?
a: Your ARN and EUIN.

flash.q: What must accompany any past-performance figure?
a: The standard mutual fund risk disclaimer. Never promise or imply guaranteed returns or recovery timelines.

flash.q: What is the complaint escalation path you share with clients?
a: AMC → SEBI SCORES → Smart ODR. Escalate promptly and never discourage a client from complaining.

flash.q: Key compliance don'ts?
a: Deal with clients before NISM V-A + EUIN
Call yourself an adviser or charge a fee
Sell above the client's risk level
Hide costs or churn for commission
Accept cash or handle client money

quiz.why: An independent custodian holds the fund's securities. Investor money is never held by the AMC or the distributor.

quiz.q: Which body registers mutual fund distributors and issues the ARN?
quiz.why: AMFI is the industry body that registers distributors (ARN). SEBI is the regulator.

quiz.q: Who needs an EUIN?
o: Only the head of the distribution firm
Only employees handling lump sums above ₹1 lakh
Every employee who deals with clients
quiz.why: Each person dealing with clients needs NISM Series V-A and an EUIN, quoted on every transaction they handle.

quiz.q: Why is a regular plan's expense ratio higher than a direct plan's?
o: It includes the distributor's trail commission
It pays a higher fund-manager salary
It includes stamp duty on every purchase
quiz.why: The regular plan carries the trail commission, paid only while the client stays invested and shown in the CAS.

Allowed once a year at the annual review

quiz.why: The foundation check comes first. If it is missing, fixing it is the first recommendation.

quiz.q: A wealthy client with high risk capacity panics and sells in every market fall. How should they be profiled?

Aggressive, to make up for past losses
quiz.why: Recommendations follow the LOWER of capacity and tolerance. Low tolerance sets the limit.

quiz.q: "How much risk the goal actually requires" describes:
quiz.why: Risk need compares the goal amount with current savings and time left.

quiz.q: Which discovery question reveals the most about risk tolerance?
o: "How many bank accounts do you have?"
"What happened during the last market fall?"

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four things captured for every goal?
o: The fund the client has already chosen

quiz.q: A client has ₹20 lakh for a 10-year goal but fears investing at the wrong time. Best method?
o: STP from a liquid/debt fund into equity over 6–12 months
Invest all of it in small-cap today
Keep it in a savings account until markets fall
quiz.why: STP stages a large sum into equity and reduces timing regret.

quiz.q: Which is NOT part of the onboarding checklist?
o: Riskometer matched to the client's profile
quiz.why: Returns are never guaranteed. Promising them is a compliance breach.

quiz.q: An SWP is best suited for:
o: Building a corpus from monthly income
Moving money between two equity funds
quiz.why: SWP provides regular withdrawals; SIP is for accumulation from income.

quiz.why: A yearly structured review is where most long-term value is added.

quiz.why: XIRR accounts for each instalment's date. CAGR is for a single lump sum.

A friend's fund returned 40% last year
quiz.why: Other valid reasons are a manager/style change, a mandate change, or a change in the client's goal.

quiz.q: ₹10,000/month at an assumed 12% for 20 years, stepped up 10% every year, ends at about:
quiz.why: A flat SIP ends at ≈₹1 Cr. The 10% step-up nearly doubles it to ≈₹1.99 Cr (illustration only).

quiz.q: Before recommending any switch, the distributor must always check:

Whether the new fund is an NFO
quiz.why: A switch is a redemption plus a purchase, so it can trigger exit load and tax.

quiz.q: Markets fall 15%. What is the first thing you do?

quiz.why: Call first, before clients call in panic, and reconnect them to their goals.

quiz.why: The buying price doesn't affect what the fund does next. Ask if it's still the right fund for the goal.

quiz.q: "My friend's fund gave 40%. Let's switch." Which bias is this?
quiz.why: Respond by comparing both funds over 5 years, including how each did in bad years.

o: The same instalment buys more units

No, switches within one fund house are tax-free
Only if the amount exceeds ₹1 lakh

intro: PMS is a concentrated, high-ticket product held in the client's own name, so a PMS distributor's job is due diligence and suitability first, and access second. This manual trains Fund Horizon's new employees and sales team to do that at every stage of the client relationship.

blocks.text: A PMS is a professionally managed portfolio of securities held directly in the client's own demat account, regulated by SEBI, with a minimum investment of ₹50 lakh.

items: Discretionary: the portfolio manager decides what to buy and sell. This is the most common type.

Advisory: the manager only advises; the client executes.
Portfolios are concentrated, typically 15–30 stocks, so they can differ sharply from the index, both up and down.
Since April 2023, every PMS investment approach is grouped under one of four strategies (equity, debt, hybrid, multi-asset) and compared against a common benchmark, with data published through APMI.

subs.title: Fee structures, with a worked example

blocks.text: PMS fees are set in the agreement and usually take one of three forms: fixed (a flat % of assets a year), performance-linked (a share of profits above a hurdle rate, usually with a high-water mark), or hybrid (a lower fixed fee plus a profit share). Operating expenses, excluding brokerage, are capped at 0.5% a year.
Illustration on a ₹1 crore portfolio (hypothetical, before GST, brokerage and operating expenses):

rows: Year's gross return
Option A: 2.5% fixed
Option B: 1% fixed + 20% of gains above a 10% hurdle
Fee ₹2.5 L → net gain ₹15.5 L
Fee ₹1 L + 20% of ₹8 L = ₹2.6 L → net gain ₹15.4 L
Fee ₹2.5 L → net loss ₹12.5 L
Fee ₹1 L, no profit share → net loss ₹11 L

blocks.text: The high-water mark means that after a loss year, the profit share is charged only on gains above the portfolio's previous peak, so the client does not pay twice for recovering the same ground.

script.title: The PMS Distributor
script.text: Welcome to Module 2 of the Fund Horizon training series: the PMS Distributor. Portfolio Management Services are a concentrated, high-ticket product held in the client's own name. So our job is due diligence and suitability first, and access second. We'll follow the same L.E.A.R.N. framework as Module 1: Learn the basics, Evaluate the client, Act right, Review and rebalance, and Navigate behaviour.

script.title: L.E.A.R.N. applied to PMS
script.text: Here's how L.E.A.R.N. applies to PMS. Learn: what a PMS is, and who is allowed to sell it. Evaluate: the most important idea in this module is that being eligible for PMS is not the same as being suitable for it. Act right: proper due diligence on the strategy, and fees explained in rupees, not percentages. Review: judge a PMS on after-fee returns against its benchmark. And Navigate: concentrated portfolios fall harder, so keeping clients steady matters even more than with mutual funds.

script.title: What a PMS is, in three numbers
script.text: A Portfolio Management Service is a professionally managed portfolio held directly in the client's own demat account, regulated by SEBI. Remember three numbers. Fifty lakh rupees is the SEBI minimum. Fifteen to thirty stocks is a typical portfolio, much more concentrated than a mutual fund. And one demat account in the client's own name, so they can see every stock and every trade. There are three types: discretionary, where the manager decides every trade, and which is the most common; non-discretionary, where the client approves each trade; and advisory, where the manager only advises. Since April 2023, every PMS approach is grouped into one of four strategies, equity, debt, hybrid or multi-asset, and compared against a common benchmark, with data published through APMI.

script.title: Mutual fund, PMS or AIF?
script.text: Clients often ask how PMS differs from mutual funds and AIFs. Focus on the PMS column. The minimum is fifty lakh rupees, against a few hundred for a mutual fund and typically one crore for an AIF. In a PMS, the client owns the shares directly in their own demat, rather than units of a pooled fund. Some customisation is possible, like excluding a stock. Tax is different: every sale by the manager is a taxable event in the client's own hands. Fees are fixed, profit-linked, or a mix. And the client sees every holding and every trade. Those last two points, tax and visibility, are where most client surprises come from.

script.title: Three steps before selling any PMS
script.text: Before anyone at Fund Horizon talks to a client about PMS, three things must be in place. First, the NISM Series XXI-A PMS Distributors certification. Second, registration with APMI and an APRN, the APMI Registration Number. Since 31st July 2025, distributors without an APRN cannot bring in new PMS business or receive commission. Third, an EUIN for each employee of a non-individual distributor. Two more rules shape every conversation: we earn trail commission only, never upfront; and every client can choose to onboard directly with the portfolio manager. So we must be clear about the value we add.

script.title: Eligible is not the same as suitable
script.text: This is the most important idea in the module: meeting the fifty lakh minimum makes a client eligible, not suitable. Look at the first client. They have about three crore invested: an emergency and debt cushion, a solid mutual fund core, some other holdings, and PMS as a seventeen percent slice on top. That's suitable. Now the second client: fifty-five lakh in total savings, and they want fifty lakh of it in PMS. That's ninety-one percent of everything they have, with no core portfolio and no emergency buffer. They are eligible, but this is a red flag. For them, the right advice is mutual funds first, PMS later.

script.title: Five suitability checks
script.text: Use these five checks with every PMS prospect. Surplus: the fifty lakh should be a slice of a larger portfolio, not most of their wealth. Core portfolio: they should already have mutual funds, debt and an emergency fund; PMS should never be someone's first equity investment. Horizon: three to five years or more without needing the money. Drawdowns: ask what they did in March 2020. If they stayed invested through a thirty percent fall, good. If they've never seen one, or sold in one, be careful. And tax: they must understand that every trade the manager makes is taxed in their hands. A useful question to ask: "If this portfolio fell thirty percent in a year while the Nifty fell fifteen, how would you react?"

script.title: Fewer stocks, bigger bets
script.text: Here's why PMS behaves so differently from a mutual fund or an index. The Nifty 50 spreads money across fifty stocks. A typical PMS holds about twenty, so each stock carries far more weight. When the manager is right, that concentration can beat the index by a wide margin. When the manager is wrong, or the style is out of favour, it can lag by a wide margin too. Every PMS client must understand this before they invest: the same concentration that creates the upside creates the downside.

script.title: Due diligence before any recommendation
script.text: Stage three is Act right, and in PMS it starts with due diligence. This is where we earn our trail. Check eight things before recommending any strategy. Track record: after-fee returns over three, five and seven years, including how it did in the 2020 and 2022 falls. Manager and team: who runs the money, and for how long. Process: the style, and whether it's applied consistently. Portfolio: number of stocks, how much sits in the top ten, sector tilts. Risk: the worst fall, volatility, and how long recovery took. Costs: every fee, the exit load, and expected trading churn. Documents: the Disclosure Document and the agreement. And always compare two or three strategies in the same category using APMI's published data.

script.title: Fees, shown in rupees, in good and bad years
script.text: Clients understand fees in rupees, not percentages, so always show them this way. Take a one crore portfolio and two fee options. Option A charges a flat 2.5% a year. Option B charges 1% fixed plus 20% of gains above a 10% hurdle. In a good year, with an 18% gross return, they cost almost the same: two and a half lakh versus two point six lakh, leaving a net gain of about fifteen and a half lakh either way. But in a bad year, with a 10% fall, Option A still charges two and a half lakh, while Option B charges only the one lakh fixed fee. So the client loses twelve and a half lakh with A, and eleven lakh with B. Neither is always better; what matters is that the client sees both years before choosing. This is a hypothetical example, before GST, brokerage and operating expenses.

script.title: How a high-water mark protects the client
script.text: When a PMS charges a share of profits, ask whether it uses a high-water mark, and explain it like this. Say a client's portfolio grows from one crore to one crore twenty lakh in year one. That's a new peak, so the manager earns a profit share. In year two it falls back to one crore, and in year three it recovers to one fifteen. With a high-water mark, no profit share is charged in those years, because the client is only regaining lost ground. In year four it reaches one thirty-five, and the profit share applies only to the fifteen lakh above the old peak of one twenty. Without a high-water mark, the client could pay twice for the same gains. Always check the agreement for when and how the high-water mark resets.

script.title: The PMS onboarding checklist
script.text: Before the client signs, run this checklist. Suitability documented and signed. The Disclosure Document shared and its key risks explained. The agreement, fee schedule and exit load reviewed together. Fees shown in rupees for an up year and a down year. The direct onboarding option mentioned, and our role explained. KYC, demat and bank accounts opened in the client's own name. The scope of the DDPI or power of attorney explained before signing. A nominee added to the PMS demat account. And our APRN and EUIN on every document, with the trail commission disclosed. Then set expectations honestly: show how the manager did in past falls, and what the client would pay in a good year and a bad one.

script.title: Strategy return is not your return
script.text: This is the most common PMS review complaint: "The factsheet says forty percent, so why have I only made twelve?" Look at the chart. The strategy launched at one hundred and is at one forty today. Client A joined at launch and is up forty percent. Client B joined at month twelve, after a strong run, at one twenty-five, and is up only twelve percent. Same strategy, same fees, different entry point. In every review, show the client their own account's return after all fees, against the benchmark over the same period, not the strategy's headline number. These are hypothetical values for illustration.

script.title: Stay, or review for exit?
script.text: When should a client leave a PMS? Use these signals. One year behind the benchmark, with the process unchanged and the style simply out of favour: stay, and explain the style cycle. Behind both the benchmark and peers for three years or more: review for exit. Style drift, where the manager is no longer doing what was sold: review, because it's no longer the product the client bought. A change in the client's own goals, horizon or liquidity needs: re-check suitability. And if the fund manager or key team leaves: review immediately. Before recommending any exit, always show the client the exit load, the tax on gains, and the cost of rebuilding elsewhere. Talk-track: "After all fees, your account is three percent a year ahead of its benchmark over three years. The manager and process are unchanged, so we stay."

script.title: The playbook for a sharp fall
script.text: The emotional test is sharper in PMS than in mutual funds, for four reasons: bigger swings from a concentrated portfolio; full visibility, so clients see every stock in red in their own demat; switching costs real tax; and wealthy clients constantly hear about last year's top PMS. So follow this playbook. One, set expectations at onboarding by showing the strategy's worst past fall. Two, call clients before they call you, newest clients first. Three, separate a market-wide fall from a problem with the manager. Four, check the process, not the price: if the manager and process are intact, the case for staying holds. Five, show the cost of leaving: tax, exit load, and the risk of selling at the low. Six, record the conversation and follow up in writing.

script.title: When the PMS client says…
script.text: Here are three things PMS clients often say. "This stock is down forty percent, tell the manager to sell it." That's loss aversion and the illusion of control. Respond: you're paying the manager for the whole portfolio, so let's judge the portfolio against its benchmark, not one stock. "My friend's PMS made sixty percent last year, let's move." That's recency and herd behaviour. Respond: let's compare both on after-fee returns over five years, including their worst year. "The market is up, but my PMS isn't." That's short-term framing. Respond: this style lags in some phases, so here's how it did across a full cycle. And when a dip is within what you discussed at onboarding, say so: exiting now would lock in both the loss and the tax.

script.title: What PMS clients miss, and complain about later
script.text: These are the niche topics that drive most PMS complaints later. A client's own return differs from the strategy's published return because of entry timing. Hidden costs, like brokerage, custody charges and GST on fees, add up beyond the headline fee. Every trade is taxed in the client's hands, so high churn can mean a bigger tax bill; involve their CA. Exit loads are capped by SEBI at up to 3%, 2% and 1% in the first three years. The direct onboarding option is always available, so explain our value. Many providers let clients fund a PMS with shares they already own. Clients should know exactly what the DDPI authorises. And they should add a nominee to the PMS demat account too.

script.title: Eligible is not the same as suitable.
script.text: If you remember one thing from this module, remember this: eligible is not the same as suitable. Fifty lakh rupees opens the door to PMS. Our job is to decide, honestly, whether the client should walk through it.

script.title: Dos and don'ts
script.text: Finally, compliance. Do: hold NISM XXI-A and a valid APRN; document suitability for every client; explain every fee in rupees; show returns net of fees, against the benchmark and peers; mention the direct onboarding option; record the reasons for every recommendation and exit; and share the escalation path for complaints. Don't: source PMS business without an APRN; treat the fifty lakh minimum as proof of suitability; quote headline or pre-fee returns; cherry-pick periods or strategies; take or imply upfront commission; recommend switches for commission; or promise returns or recovery timelines.

script.title: Practise, then prove it
script.text: That brings us to the end of Module 2. Practise in pairs with the six PMS role-play scenarios from the training manual, then take the ten-question quiz. The pass mark is eight out of ten. Our next module covers Investor Psychology. Thank you.

flash.q: What does "track record" due diligence look at?
a: After-fee returns vs benchmark over 3, 5 and 7 years, including how the strategy did in falls such as 2020 and 2022.

flash.q: What does "portfolio" due diligence look at?
a: Number of stocks, top-10 weight, sector and market-cap concentration, and cash calls.

flash.q: What are the three PMS fee structures?
a: Fixed: a flat % of assets a year
Performance-linked: share of profits above a hurdle, usually with a high-water mark
Hybrid: lower fixed fee plus a profit share

flash.q: What is the cap on PMS operating expenses?
a: 0.5% a year, excluding brokerage.

flash.q: Fee example, ₹1 Cr, +18% year: A = 2.5% fixed; B = 1% + 20% above a 10% hurdle?
a: A: fee ₹2.5 L → net gain ₹15.5 L. B: ₹1 L + 20% of ₹8 L = ₹2.6 L → net gain ₹15.4 L. Almost the same. (Hypothetical, before GST, brokerage and expenses.)

flash.q: Same fee options in a −10% year (₹10 L loss)?
a: A: still ₹2.5 L fee → net loss ₹12.5 L. B: only the ₹1 L fixed fee → net loss ₹11 L. Show the client both years before choosing.

flash.q: What is a high-water mark?
a: Profit share is charged only on gains above the portfolio's previous peak, so the client does not pay twice for recovering the same ground.

flash.q: High-water mark example: ₹1 Cr → ₹1.20 Cr → ₹1 Cr → ₹1.15 Cr → ₹1.35 Cr. Where is profit share charged?
a: Year 1 (new peak of ₹1.20 Cr). None in years 2–3 (regaining lost ground). Year 4 only on the ₹15 L above the old ₹1.20 Cr peak.

flash.q: The PMS onboarding checklist?
a: Suitability documented and signed
Disclosure Document shared; risks explained
Agreement, fee schedule, exit load reviewed
Fee illustration in rupees: up, flat, down years
Direct option mentioned; our role explained
KYC, demat, bank in client's name
DDPI / POA scope explained · Nominee added
APRN & EUIN on documents; trail disclosed

flash.q: How is a PMS judged?
a: On at least 3 years of after-fee returns against its benchmark, never on one quarter or on the strategy's headline number.

flash.q: The PMS review rhythm?
a: Monthly: statement; check unusual trades, cash, drawdowns
Quarterly: call/note on performance vs benchmark, changes, manager commentary
Annually: full review with the client

flash.q: The annual review agenda?
a: Client update · Returns (own account, after fees)
Risk (largest fall vs benchmark)
Portfolio (concentration, turnover, drift, cash)
Manager changes · Costs in ₹ and tax
Fit as a share of total portfolio
Decision: stay, top up, reduce or exit, with reasons

flash.q: "Factsheet says 40%, why have I only made 12%?"
a: Entry timing. Client A joined at launch (100 → 140, up 40%); Client B joined at 125 after a strong run (up 12%). Show the client's own after-fee account return vs benchmark for the same period.

flash.q: Lagging benchmark for 1 year, process unchanged, style out of favour?
a: Stay, and explain the style cycle.

flash.q: Lagging benchmark AND peers for 3+ years?
a: Review for exit.

flash.q: The fund manager or key team leaves?
a: Review immediately. Proactively inform the client; no panic and no automatic exit.

flash.q: Style drift away from what was sold?
a: Review. It is no longer the product the client bought.

flash.q: What must be set out before any PMS exit?
a: The exit load, the tax on gains, and the cost of rebuilding elsewhere.

flash.q: Why is the emotional test harder in PMS than in MFs?
a: Bigger swings from 15–30 stocks
Full visibility: every red stock in their own demat
Switching costs real tax and exit load
Peer talk about "last year's top PMS"

flash.q: The 6-step playbook for a sharp fall or long underperformance?
a: Set expectations at onboarding (show worst past fall)
Call before they call, newest clients first
Separate the market from the manager
Check the process, not the price
Show the cost of leaving (tax, exit load, selling low)
Record and follow up in writing

flash.q: "This stock is down 40%, tell the manager to sell it." Bias and response?
a: Loss aversion and illusion of control. "You're paying the manager for the whole portfolio. Let's judge the portfolio against its benchmark, not one stock."

flash.q: "My friend's PMS made 60% last year. Let's move." Bias and response?
a: Recency and herd. "Let's compare both on after-fee returns over five years, including their worst year."

flash.q: "The market is up but my PMS isn't." Bias and response?
a: Short-term framing. "This style lags in some phases. Here's how it did across a full cycle."

flash.q: Talk-track when a dip is within what was discussed at onboarding?
a: "This dip is within what we discussed at the start. Exiting now would lock in both the loss and the tax."

flash.q: Why can a client's return differ from the published strategy return?
a: Each portfolio is built at a different time and price, with different cash flows. Ask for your own account's after-fee return.

flash.q: What hidden costs sit beyond the headline fee?
a: Brokerage, custody and demat charges, and GST on fees and profit share. Ask for the all-in cost.

flash.q: How does manager turnover affect the client's tax?
a: Every sale is a capital gains event for the client, so high turnover can mean a bigger tax bill. Tax on PMS fees is not straightforward; involve the client's CA.

flash.q: What are the SEBI caps on PMS exit loads?
a: Up to 3% in year 1, 2% in year 2 and 1% in year 3. The actual load is set in each agreement.

flash.q: What is an in-specie transfer?
a: Many providers accept existing shares instead of cash, and can return securities instead of selling on exit. Check the provider's policy.

flash.q: Why does the DDPI / POA scope matter?
a: The authority signed over the demat and bank account defines what the manager can do. Read what you authorise before signing.

flash.q: Nomination and corporate actions in a PMS?
a: Nominee, dividends, bonuses and voting rights all sit in the client's own demat. Add a nominee to the PMS demat too.

flash.q: What to ask about high-water marks and cash flows?
a: Whether and when the high-water mark resets, and whether fees are charged on contributions or withdrawals.

flash.q: Top-ups and partial withdrawals?
a: Rules on minimum top-ups and partial withdrawals vary by provider and agreement. Know them before the money is needed.

flash.q: What must be in place before dealing with PMS clients?
a: NISM XXI-A certification and a valid APRN (plus EUIN for employees of non-individual distributors).

flash.q: How must PMS performance be shown?
a: Net of fees, against the benchmark and peers. Never quote headline or pre-fee returns, or cherry-pick periods or strategies.

flash.q: The PMS complaint escalation path?
a: Provider → SEBI SCORES → Smart ODR.

flash.q: Key PMS compliance don'ts?
a: Source PMS business without an APRN
Treat ₹50 L as proof of suitability
Take or imply upfront commission or fees
Recommend switches for commission
Promise returns or recovery timelines
